analysis.one_liner: Adds an income test that pushes higher-earning debtors out of full bankruptcy forgiveness into court-supervised repayment plans.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 107th Congress with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to two committees, never received a markup or a vote, and died when that Congress ended on January 3, 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites federal bankruptcy law around a 'needs-based' test: if a debtor's income exceeds their state's median (after certain expenses), their case carries a presumption of abuse and they can be pushed from Chapter 7, which wipes out most debts, into Chapter 13, which requires a multi-year repayment plan. Before filing, debtors would have to complete credit counseling from an approved agency and a financial management course, and debt-relief agencies and petition preparers would face new restrictions and penalties. The bill also carries a long list of other changes: it permanently renews Chapter 12 protection for family farmers and adds family fishermen, gives priority and near-absolute protection to child support and alimony claims, adds disclosure and enforcement rules aimed at abusive creditor and reaffirmation practices, shields retirement and education savings, adds patient protections when a health care business goes bankrupt, strengthens protections for secured creditors, and requires new credit card and lending disclosures.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumer lenders — chiefly credit card issuers holding unsecured debts — gain the most, since the income test forces more debtors into repayment plans instead of discharging what they owe. Secured creditors like mortgage and auto lenders gain from new rules that speed relief from the automatic stay and improve their treatment in Chapter 13. Credit counseling agencies gain a government-mandated stream of customers. Family farmers and fishermen gain permanent access to Chapter 12, and custodial parents gain priority status for support claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card issuers and secured lenders

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates a formula-based presumption of abuse — and possible dismissal or conversion — when a debtor's income above IRS-standard expenses leaves enough over 60 months to repay a set share of unsecured debts, moving higher-income debtors from Chapter 7 discharge into Chapter 13 repayment.

It requires every individual debtor to receive credit counseling from an approved nonprofit agency within 180 days before filing, and to complete a financial management course before receiving a discharge.
It makes domestic support obligations a top priority claim, gives them special collection powers, and makes most alimony and child support debts nondischargeable.
It permanently reenacts Chapter 12 for family farmers, raises its debt limit, and extends the same protection to family fishermen.

It lets courts cut creditors' claims by up to 20 percent when they unreasonably refuse a debtor's pre-bankruptcy repayment offer, and imposes new disclosure requirements on reaffirmation agreements, where debtors agree to keep paying a debt after bankruptcy.

It protects retirement savings and education savings from the bankruptcy estate, protects personally identifiable information, appoints a privacy ombudsman, and adds patient-advocate rules when an insolvent health care business closes.
It requires new credit disclosures on introductory rates, internet card solicitations, late-payment penalties, and open-end credit plans.

analysis.who_pays: Debtors seeking a fresh start — especially middle-income households above their state's median — would face a presumption of abuse, mandatory counseling costs, stricter expense standards pegged to IRS tables rather than actual costs, longer waits between discharges, and homestead exemption limits. Bankruptcy attorneys and petition preparers would face fee liability and civil penalties for filings later found abusive. Debtors who might have erased their debts would instead spend years repaying a portion to lenders.

drawbacks.text: The means test replaces a judge's case-by-case judgment with a rigid formula: abuse is presumed whenever the arithmetic triggers it, and the debtor can only escape by documenting 'special circumstances' expense by expense under oath. Debtors below their state's median income are protected from most such motions, but many above-median households facing job loss, medical bills, or divorce would be steered into repayment plans they cannot realistically sustain.
The mandatory credit counseling requirement adds a gatekeeping step and cost before a debtor can even file, with only narrow waivers for emergencies or districts with inadequate agencies.

New restrictions on 'debt relief agencies' and a penalty on persons who negligently or fraudulently prepare bankruptcy petitions raise the cost and risk for the lawyers and preparers that struggling debtors depend on, which would likely push up legal fees or leave some debtors unrepresented.

Several provisions strengthen creditors' positions — fair treatment for secured creditors in Chapter 13, prompt relief from the automatic stay when debtors fail to surrender collateral, a five-year Chapter 13 duration in some cases, longer periods between discharges, and limits on the homestead exemption — shifting leverage and value from debtors to lenders.
The bill would raise filing fees for the United States trustee program, a direct cost added to bankruptcy cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The package is genuinely two bills in one. Its consumer-protection titles are real: child support priority, farmer and fisherman protection, reaffirmation disclosures, retirement-savings protection, and credit-disclosure rules would all help ordinary people. But its centerpiece — the needs-based income test, mandatory counseling, and attorney-liability regime — is the part the consumer credit industry had sought for years, and it systematically moves the cost of financial failure from lenders onto debtors. The consumer protections are layered onto a core that restricts bankruptcy relief; on balance the bill's main effect would be to make debt relief harder to get for middle-income households while leaving the industry that extended the credit largely untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on November 14, 2002, referred to the Judiciary and Financial Services committees, and neither committee ever acted on it — no markup, no vote — so it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas introduced the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2002 on November 14, 2002, in the closing weeks of the 107th Congress.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Financial Services Committee.
Neither committee took any further action — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2003, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer debtors are better off that it died, since the existing, more flexible bankruptcy law stayed in place; the credit card and lending industries did not get the income test and counseling regime they wanted from this bill. Custodial parents and family farmers also gained nothing, because the bill's genuine protections for them died with it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer debtors, who kept the old rules

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: The income test, mandatory counseling, and longer repayment obligations are aimed at debtors who owe these lenders money, converting debts that would have been discharged into years of repayment. Their gain comes directly out of debtors' pockets.

industries.industry: Secured creditors (mortgage, auto, and other collateralized lenders)
industries.note: The bill gives secured creditors fair treatment in Chapter 13, prompt relief from the automatic stay, fair valuation of collateral, and curbs on abusive filings, strengthening their claims at debtors' expense.

The mandatory pre-filing counseling requirement makes government-approved nonprofit agencies the gate every debtor must pass through, creating a guaranteed customer base. The bill imposes approval standards and liability rules on them, but the mandate locks in their role.

The bill restricts debt relief agencies, requires attorney certifications on every filing, and lets courts order attorneys to reimburse trustees for costs when a case is found abusive, raising their risk. Since these professionals work for debtors, their interest runs with the public's.
Chapter 12 protection for family farmers would be permanently reenacted with a higher debt limit, and family fishermen would be brought within the same protection for the first time.
Title IX would give qualified financial contracts at failing insured depository institutions special treatment outside normal bankruptcy processes, insulating those deals from the estate.
